A rock is launched vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth and an identical rock is
launched vertically upwards from the surface of Mars. Each rock is launched with an initial
velocity of 12 m s–1.
Each rock then reaches its maximum height above the surface before returning back down to the
surface. The velocity–time graph for each rock is shown. In both cases, air resistance is
negligible.

hints: Notice where each velocity-time line crosses $v = 0$ - that time marks maximum height because upward motion stops there.
Recall that displacement is the area under a velocity-time graph, so maximum height is the area of the small triangle above the time axis from $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to zero.
Read the time to $v = 0$ for Earth at about $1.2 \text{ s}$ and for Mars at about $3.2 \text{ s}$, then compare $\frac{1}{2} \times base \times height$ for the two triangles.
walkthrough: Maximum height is reached when upward velocity becomes zero, so read the time where each graph crosses the time axis.
Displacement equals area under the velocity-time graph, so height $h = $ area of triangle with vertical side $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and base equal to time to $v=0$.
For Earth, time to zero is about $1.2 \text{ s}$, so $h_{Earth} = \frac{1}{2} \times 1.2 \times 12 = 7.2 \text{ m}$.
For Mars, time to zero is about $3.2 \text{ s}$, so $h_{Mars} = \frac{1}{2} \times 3.2 \times 12 = 19.2 \text{ m}$.
Difference $= 19.2 - 7.2 = 12 \text{ m}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Difference of the two triangular areas is about $19.2 - 7.2 = 12 \text{ m}$.

B.explanation: This is close to the Mars maximum height alone, not the difference between Mars and Earth heights.

C.explanation: This is the Mars maximum height of about $19.2 \text{ m}$, not the difference.

D.explanation: This is too large and would need a much longer time to reach zero velocity on Mars.
